Roger Sharpe demonstrates to the NYC City Council that pinball is a game of skill and not chance, leading to its decriminalization. 1976

Pinball was banned beginning in the early 1940s until 1976 in New York City and many other American cities. As it was seen as a game of chance and not skill it was classified as illegal gambling. New York mayor La Guardia was responsible for the ban and participated with police in destroying machines with sledgehammers before dumping the remnants into the city's rivers.

The ban ended when Roger Sharpe testified in April 1976 before a City Council committee in a Manhattan courtroom that pinball games were games of skill and not games of chance. He played games on two pinball machines set up in the courtroom, and – in a move he compares to Babe Ruth's home run in the 1932 World Series – called out precisely what he was going to shoot for and then proceeded to do so. Astonished committee members immediately voted to remove the ban, which was followed in other cities. Source.

Sharpe is still ranked as the #277 pinball player in the world. His sons Zach Sharpe and Josh Sharpe are #5 and #19 in the world, respectively. Source.
